divisions.question: That the amendments be disagreed to.
Alan Ferguson The question is that opposition amendments (62) to (64) and (66) to (68) on sheet 5684 be agreed to.

Consideration resumed. Alan Ferguson The committee is considering the [Nation-building Funds Bill 2008](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/R3099) and Senator Milne’s amendment (1) on sheet 5645. The question is that Senator Milne’s amendments be agreed to. Nick Sherry The existing evaluation principles for the funds provide an appropriate framework for expenditure. They require projects to address national infrastructure priorities, demonstrate high benefits and effective use of resources, efficiently address infrastructure needs and demonstrate that they achieved established standards in the implementation of management. The principles enable environmental considerations to be assessed as appropriate, such as evaluating benefits and the costs of the projects. The bill provides for appropriate parliamentary scrutiny of the evaluation criteria for each fund, which will be tabled in parliament as disallowable legislative instruments. Therefore, on balance, we will not be supporting the Greens amendments. Nick Xenophon I am quite sympathetic to the Greens amendments. I understand what Senator Milne and the Greens are trying to achieve. I cannot support it, because I believe it is too prescriptive. But I urge the government to give a commitment that, when considering these nation-building funds and these projects, there will be clear criteria to achieve the goals of reducing greenhouse gases and to take climate change into account. If those criteria are not taken into account then these funds could be used for projects that are contrary to the goals that the government has espoused for dealing with carbon pollution. Nick Sherry Obviously, the evaluation of projects under the nation-building funds will conform to broader government policy. I think the most obvious area is the area of climate change. speeches.speaker: Annette Hurley
speeches.brief: The Senate Standing Committee on Economics report on the Nation‑building Funds Bill 2008, the Nation‑building Funds (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2008, and the COAG Reform Fund Bill 2008 was presented, and ordered to be printed.

speeches.speaker: Chris Evans
speeches.brief: The government introduced the Nation-building Funds Bill 2008 and related bills to establish three new infrastructure funds—Building Australia Fund, Education Investment Fund, and Health and Hospitals Fund—with contributions of $8.2 billion in 2008-09, managed by the Future Fund Board of Guardians and subject to independent evaluation, while the COAG Reform Fund was created to channel payments to states and territories.

speeches.speaker: Nick Minchin
speeches.brief: The Coalition argued the Nation-building Funds were built on Howard government surpluses, criticised Labor for raiding the Communications Fund, and warned the funds risked state cost-shifting and fiscal uncertainty; the Greens argued the funds must prioritise climate change and peak oil through amendments, and proposed a joint parliamentary committee for accountability.

speeches.speaker: Christine Milne
speeches.brief: The speaker moved amendments to establish a Parliamentary Joint Committee on Nation‑Building to scrutinise infrastructure spending over $50 million, require ministers to table written reasons for payment recommendations, and preserve the Communications Fund for rural and regional telecommunications.

speeches.speaker: Alan Ferguson
speeches.brief: Senator Milne argued that nation‑building fund projects should include mandatory criteria for climate change mitigation, adaptation and peak oil preparation, and moved amendments to that effect. Her amendment requiring Infrastructure Australia’s advice to be tabled in Parliament was agreed to, but the climate‑ and peak‑oil‑related amendments were rejected.
